reminder: A rational point of a [variety](c:algebraic-variety) is a point whose coordinates are all [rational numbers](c:rational-number).
definition: A rational point of an [algebraic variety](c:algebraic-variety) cut out by [polynomial](c:polynomial) equations over $\mathbb{Q}$ is a [solution](c:solution) of these equations whose coordinates are all [rational numbers](c:rational-number). In scheme language, a rational point of an [arithmetic scheme](c:arithmetic-scheme) $S$ is a morphism $\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{Q})\to S$.
examples: The point $(3/5,\,4/5)$ is a rational point of the unit circle $x^2+y^2=1$.
The points $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$ and $(-1,0)$ are rational points of the curve $y^2=x^3-x$.
Non-example: The point $(1/\sqrt2,\,1/\sqrt2)$ lies on the unit circle, but its coordinates are not rational.

reminder: A Euclidean theory is reflection positive when an observable paired with its own time reflection has non-negative expectation.
definition: A Euclidean quantum field theory is reflection positive when $\langle\overline{\Theta F}\,F\rangle\ge0$ for every observable $F$ that depends only on fields at positive Euclidean time, where $\Theta$ reflects Euclidean time. This positivity lets the Osterwalder-Schrader reconstruction build a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) of states, and it gives [unitarity](c:unitarity) of the real-time theory after [Wick rotation](c:wick-rotation).
examples: The Gaussian process with covariance $e^{-m|t|}$, the Euclidean harmonic oscillator, is reflection positive, since $\sum_{i,j}c_ic_je^{-m(t_i+t_j)}=\big(\sum_ic_ie^{-mt_i}\big)^2\ge0$ for $t_i>0$.
The free Euclidean scalar field with covariance $(-\Delta+m^2)^{-1}$ is reflection positive, and its reconstruction is the free relativistic field.
Non-example: A Gaussian process with covariance $\cos t$ is not reflection positive, because $\langle X_{-\pi/2}X_{\pi/2}\rangle=\cos\pi=-1<0$.

reminder: The Riemann sphere is the complex plane with one point at infinity added, forming a sphere.
definition: The Riemann sphere is the [2-sphere](c:2-sphere) with its structure of a one-dimensional [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold). It is the set of [complex numbers](c:complex-number) with one added point $\infty$, using the chart $z$ near finite points and the chart $1/z$ near $\infty$, and it is the complex [projective line](c:projective-line).
examples: A rational function such as $f(z)=(z-1)/(z+1)$ is a holomorphic map from the Riemann sphere to itself, with $f(-1)=\infty$ and $f(\infty)=1$.
The biholomorphic self-maps of the Riemann sphere are the Möbius maps $z\mapsto(az+b)/(cz+d)$ with $ad-bc\ne0$.
Non-example: The plane $\mathbb C$ is not the Riemann sphere, because it lacks the point $\infty$ and is not compact.

steps: Take $n=1$ in [complex projective space](c:complex-projective-space), the set of complex lines through $0$ in $\mathbb C^{n+1}$.
Send the line through $(z_0,z_1)$ to the ratio $z_0/z_1$, and to $\infty$ when $z_1=0$.
This bijection onto the Riemann sphere matches the projective charts $z_0/z_1$ and $z_1/z_0$ with the charts $z$ and $1/z$.
links.why: Facts about complex projective spaces, such as the action of $\mathrm{PGL}_2(\mathbb C)$ by Möbius maps, then apply to the sphere.

reminder: The Riemann zeta function adds $n^{-s}$ over all positive integers $n$, and extends to a function with one pole at $s=1$.
definition: The Riemann zeta function is $\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}$, a [series](c:series) that converges for $\mathrm{Re}\,s>1$. Its [analytic continuation](c:analytic-continuation) is a [meromorphic function](c:meromorphic-function) on the plane of [complex numbers](c:complex-number) whose only [pole](c:pole-of-a-function) is a simple pole at $s=1$ with residue $1$.
examples: At $s=2$ the series converges and $\zeta(2)=\pi^2/6$.
At $s=-1$ the series diverges, but the continuation gives $\zeta(-1)=-1/12$.
Non-example: The series $\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}$ alone is not the zeta function at $s=1/2$, because it diverges there and only the continuation has a value.

steps: A [Dirichlet series](c:dirichlet-series) has the form $\sum_{n\ge1}a_nn^{-s}$ with complex coefficients $a_n$.
Choose $a_n=1$ for every $n$.
The series then converges for $\mathrm{Re}\,s>1$ and defines $\zeta(s)$ there.
links.why: Results on convergence half-planes of Dirichlet series apply to $\zeta$.

steps: The [Dedekind zeta function](c:dedekind-zeta-function) of a [number field](c:number-field) $K$ sums $N(\mathfrak a)^{-s}$ over the nonzero ideals $\mathfrak a$ of its [ring of integers](c:ring-of-integers).
Take $K=\mathbb Q$, whose ring of integers $\mathbb Z$ has the nonzero ideals $(n)$ for $n\ge1$.
The norm of $(n)$ is $n$, so the sum becomes $\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}$, which is $\zeta(s)$.
links.why: The Riemann zeta function is the base case of the Dedekind zeta functions of number fields.

reminder: A right triangle is a [triangle](c:triangle) with one [angle](c:angle) of $90$ degrees.
definition: A right triangle is a [triangle](c:triangle) in the Euclidean [plane](c:plane) with one [angle](c:angle) equal to $90^\circ$. The side opposite the right angle is the hypotenuse, the other two sides are the legs, and the other two angles are acute.
examples: The triangle with sides $3$, $4$ and $5$ is a right triangle, because $3^2+4^2=5^2$.
Cutting a square along a diagonal gives two right triangles, each with legs $1$ and $1$ and hypotenuse $\sqrt2$ for a unit square.
Non-example: A triangle with sides $2$, $3$ and $4$ has no right angle, because $2^2+3^2=13\ne4^2$.

steps: Start with any [triangle](c:triangle) in the plane, with vertices $A$, $B$ and $C$.
Add one condition: the angle at $C$ equals $90^\circ$.
Then the other two angles are acute, because the three angles sum to $180^\circ$.
links.why: Every fact about triangles, such as the angle sum of $180^\circ$, holds for right triangles.

reminder: The second derivative of $f$ is the [derivative](c:derivative) of $f'$, and it measures how fast the slope changes.
definition: Let $f$ be a [differentiable function](c:differentiable-function) on an interval whose [derivative](c:derivative) $f'$ is again differentiable. The second derivative is $f''=(f')'$, so $f''(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f'(x+h)-f'(x)}{h}$, a [limit](c:limit-of-a-function) that must exist.
examples: For $f(x)=x^3$ we get $f'(x)=3x^2$ and $f''(x)=6x$.
For a position $s(t)$ along a line, the second derivative $s''(t)$ is the acceleration.
Non-example: $f(x)=x|x|$ has $f'(x)=2|x|$, but $f''(0)$ does not exist, because $2|x|$ has a corner at $0$.

steps: For $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$, the [Hessian](c:hessian) is the matrix of second partial derivatives $\partial^2f/\partial x_i\partial x_j$.
Take $n=1$, so the matrix has a single entry.
That entry is the second derivative $f''(x)$.
links.why: Facts about the Hessian, such as the test for convexity, reduce to the sign of $f''$ in one variable.

reminder: A sentence is a [formula](c:formula) in which every [variable](c:variable) is bound by a quantifier.
definition: A sentence of a language $L$ is a [formula](c:formula) in which every occurrence of a [variable](c:variable) is bound by a quantifier, so no variable is free. A sentence is true or false in each [structure](c:structure) for $L$, with no assignment of values to variables.
examples: In the language of ordered sets, $\forall x\,\exists y\,(x<y)$ is a sentence.
In the language of rings, $\exists x\,(x\cdot x=2)$ is a sentence: it is true in $\mathbb R$ and false in $\mathbb Q$.
Non-example: $x<y$ is a formula but not a sentence, because $x$ and $y$ occur free.

steps: Start with a [formula](c:formula) of the language, which can have free variables.
Require that every occurrence of a variable lies under a quantifier that binds it.
Such a formula has a truth value in each structure, without an assignment of values to variables.
links.why: A formula gets a truth value only after an assignment, but a sentence is true or false on its own.

reminder: A [family of sets](c:family-of-sets) shatters $A$ if every subset of $A$ equals $A\cap F$ for some set $F$ in the family.
definition: Let $\mathcal F$ be a [family of sets](c:family-of-sets), each a subset of a set $X$. The family shatters a [subset](c:subset) $A\subseteq X$ when every subset of $A$ has the form $A\cap F$ with $F\in\mathcal F$, that is, when the traces $A\cap F$ give the whole [power set](c:power-set) of $A$.
examples: The family of closed intervals of $\mathbb R$ shatters $\{1,2\}$: the traces are $\varnothing$, $\{1\}$, $\{2\}$ and $\{1,2\}$.
The power set of $X$ shatters every subset $A$ of $X$, since each $B\subseteq A$ equals $A\cap B$.
Non-example: Closed intervals do not shatter $\{1,2,3\}$, because no interval meets it in exactly $\{1,3\}$.

reminder: A signature lists the function, constant and relation symbols of a logical language, each with its arity.
definition: A signature is a set of non-logical symbols: function symbols (a constant is a function symbol of [arity](c:arity) $0$) and relation symbols, each with a fixed arity. It fixes which [formulas](c:formula) can be written, and it says which [operations](c:operation) and [predicates](c:predicate) a structure must interpret.
examples: The signature of groups has a constant $e$, a binary function symbol $\cdot$ and a unary function symbol ${}^{-1}$.
The signature of graphs has one binary relation symbol $E$ and no function symbols.
The signature of ordered rings has the constants $0$ and $1$, the binary function symbols $+$ and $\cdot$, and the binary relation symbol $<$.
Non-example: The quantifier $\forall$ and the connective $\wedge$ are logical symbols, so they do not belong to any signature.

reminder: An $n$-simplex is the [convex hull](c:convex-hull) of $n+1$ points that are [affinely independent](c:affine-independence).
definition: An $n$-simplex is the [convex hull](c:convex-hull) of $n+1$ points $v_0,\dots,v_n$ of a [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) that are [affinely independent](c:affine-independence). Its points are the combinations $\sum t_iv_i$ with $t_i\ge0$ and $\sum t_i=1$, and the $v_i$ are its vertices.
examples: A $0$-simplex is a point, a $1$-simplex is a segment, a $2$-simplex is a triangle and a $3$-simplex is a tetrahedron.
The standard $n$-simplex $\{t\in\mathbb R^{n+1}:t_i\ge0,\ \sum_it_i=1\}$ is the convex hull of the standard basis vectors.
Non-example: A square is the convex hull of four points in a plane, but four points of a plane are never affinely independent, so the square is not a simplex.

steps: Take affinely independent points $v_0,\dots,v_n$ in $\mathbb R^m$ and form their convex hull $\Delta$.
The convex hull of any points is a [convex set](c:convex-set), so $\Delta$ is convex.
Affine independence adds one condition: each point of $\Delta$ has unique barycentric coordinates $t_0,\dots,t_n$.
links.why: A simplex inherits all facts about convex sets, such as the separation of an outside point from it by a hyperplane.

reminder: A [measure](c:measure) is singular for $\nu$ when all its mass sits on a set of $\nu$-measure zero.
definition:
A [measure](c:measure) $\mu$ is singular with respect to a measure $
u$ on the same space when $\mu$ is concentrated on a [null set](c:null-set) of $
u$: some [measurable set](c:measurable-set) $A$ has $
u(A)=0$ and $\mu(A^c)=0$. A singular measure on $\mathbb R^n$ with no named reference is singular with respect to [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure).
examples: The Dirac measure $\delta_0$ is singular with respect to Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$: take $A=\{0\}$.
The Cantor measure, the Stieltjes measure of the Cantor function, is singular: it sits on the Cantor set, which has Lebesgue measure $0$, and it has no atoms.
Non-example: The measure $\mu(B)=\int_Be^{-x^2}\,dx$ is not singular with respect to Lebesgue measure, because it gives positive mass to every set of positive Lebesgue measure.

steps: Take a point $a\in\mathbb R$ and the [Dirac measure](c:dirac-measure) $\delta_a$.
The set $\{a\}$ has Lebesgue measure $0$, while $\delta_a$ gives its complement measure $0$.
So $\delta_a$ lives on a Lebesgue null set, which makes it singular.
links.why: Dirac measures are the simplest singular measures, and the definition also allows singular measures without atoms.

reminder: A function $f$ is space-constructible when some [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) writes $f(n)$ from input $1^n$ using only $O(f(n))$ space.
definition: A function $f$ on the [natural numbers](c:natural-number) with $f(n)\ge\log n$ is space-constructible when some [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) maps the string $1^n$ to the binary form of $f(n)$ using only $O(f(n))$ cells of work tape, that is, in [space](c:space-complexity) $O(f(n))$.
examples: The functions $f(n)=n$, $f(n)=n^2$ and $f(n)=2^n$ are space-constructible.
The function $f(n)=\lceil\log_2n\rceil$ is space-constructible: a binary counter run along the input gives it in space $O(\log n)$.
Non-example: The busy beaver function is not computable, so no machine can write its value in any space bound.

reminder: A spanning tree of a [connected graph](c:connected-graph) is a [tree](c:tree) inside it that reaches every [vertex](c:vertex).
definition: A spanning tree of a [connected graph](c:connected-graph) $G$ is a [subgraph](c:is-subgraph) of $G$ that is a [tree](c:tree) and contains every [vertex](c:vertex) of $G$. It has exactly $|V|-1$ edges.
examples: Deleting any one edge of a cycle $C_n$ leaves a spanning tree of $C_n$, a path through all $n$ vertices.
The complete graph $K_n$ has $n^{n-2}$ spanning trees, by Cayley's formula.
Non-example: A Hamiltonian cycle of $K_4$ contains every vertex, but it is not a spanning tree, because it contains a cycle.

steps: A [spanning subgraph](c:is-spanning-subgraph) of $G$ contains every vertex of $G$ and some of its edges.
Choose such a subgraph that is connected and has no cycle.
A connected graph without cycles is a tree, so the choice is a spanning tree.
links.why: Spanning trees inherit facts about spanning subgraphs, and the tree condition leaves exactly $|V|-1$ edges.

reminder: A spin manifold is an oriented manifold with a lift of its frame bundle to the spin group.
definition: A spin manifold is an [oriented](c:orientation-of-a-manifold) [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) $M$ with a spin structure: a principal [spin group](c:spin-group) bundle that double covers the oriented orthonormal [frame bundle](c:frame-bundle) of $M$ compatibly with the covering $\mathrm{Spin}(n)\to\mathrm{SO}(n)$. Such a structure exists exactly when the second [Stiefel-Whitney class](c:stiefel-whitney-class) $w_2(M)$ is zero.
examples: The spheres $S^n$ are spin, and so is every orientable manifold of dimension at most $3$.
The complex projective space $\mathbb{CP}^n$ is spin exactly when $n$ is odd, so $\mathbb{CP}^3$ is spin.
Non-example: The complex projective plane $\mathbb{CP}^2$ is oriented but not spin, because $w_2(\mathbb{CP}^2)\ne0$.

steps: Start with an [orientable manifold](c:orientable-manifold), which has $w_1=0$, and fix an orientation.
Add the condition that the second Stiefel-Whitney class $w_2$ vanishes.
Then the oriented frame bundle lifts through the double cover $\mathrm{Spin}(n)\to\mathrm{SO}(n)$, and a choice of lift is a spin structure.
links.why: Every spin manifold is oriented, so theorems for oriented manifolds apply, and $w_2=0$ is the extra condition.

reminder: A stationary subset of $\kappa$ has a common point with every closed unbounded subset of $\kappa$.
definition: A subset $S$ of an uncountable [regular cardinal](c:is-regular) $\kappa$ is stationary when it meets every [club set](c:club-set) in $\kappa$, that is, every closed and unbounded [subset](c:subset) of $\kappa$.
examples: Every club subset of $\omega_1$ is stationary, because two club subsets always have a common point.
The set of ordinals below $\omega_2$ of countable [cofinality](c:cofinality) is stationary in $\omega_2$.
Non-example: The set of successor ordinals below $\omega_1$ is not stationary, because the club set of limit ordinals misses it.

steps: Let $C$ be a [club set](c:club-set) in $\kappa$ and let $D$ be any club subset of $\kappa$.
For regular uncountable $\kappa$, the intersection $C\cap D$ of two club subsets is again club.
A club set is not empty, so $C$ and $D$ share a point, and $C$ is stationary.
links.why: Every club set is stationary, but a stationary set need not contain a club set.

reminder: The graph of a strictly convex function lies strictly below each chord between two points, except at the end points.
definition: A function $f$ on a [convex set](c:convex-set) $C$ is strictly convex when $f(tx+(1-t)y)<tf(x)+(1-t)f(y)$ for all $x\ne y$ in $C$ and every $t$ with $0<t<1$. It is the strict form of a [convex function](c:convex-function).
examples: The functions $x^2$ and $e^x$ are strictly convex on $\mathbb R$, and $-\log x$ is strictly convex on $(0,\infty)$.
A twice differentiable function with $f''>0$ everywhere is strictly convex.
Non-example: $f(x)=|x|$ is convex but not strictly convex, because $f(\tfrac12\cdot0+\tfrac12\cdot1)=\tfrac12=\tfrac12f(0)+\tfrac12f(1)$.

steps: A [convex function](c:convex-function) satisfies $f(tx+(1-t)y)\le tf(x)+(1-t)f(y)$ for all $x$, $y$ and $0\le t\le1$.
Replace the inequality $\le$ by the strict inequality $<$ whenever $x\ne y$ and $0<t<1$.
Every strictly convex function is convex, but $|x|$ shows that the converse fails.
links.why: Strict convexity adds uniqueness of minimizers to everything that holds for convex functions.

reminder: In the strong operator topology, a net of operators converges when it converges at every vector.
definition: The strong operator topology on the [bounded operators](c:bounded-linear-operator) on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ is the [topology](c:topology) of [pointwise convergence](c:pointwise-convergence): a net $T_\alpha$ converges to $T$ exactly when $\|T_\alpha x-Tx\|\to0$ for every $x\in H$.
examples: The coordinate projections $P_n$ on $\ell^2$ converge to the identity in the strong operator topology, but not in operator norm, since $\|I-P_n\|=1$.
The powers $(S^*)^n$ of the backward shift on $\ell^2$ converge to $0$ strongly, but not in norm.
Non-example: The powers $S^n$ of the forward shift do not converge strongly to $0$, because $\|S^nx\|=\|x\|$ for every $n$.

steps: View a bounded operator $T$ as the function $x\mapsto Tx$ from $H$ to $H$.
Give $H$ its norm topology, and use the topology of [pointwise convergence](c:pointwise-convergence) on functions $H\to H$.
Restrict this topology to the bounded operators, and call the restriction the strong operator topology.
links.why: It explains why strong convergence is weaker than norm convergence: one vector at a time is enough.

reminder: A symmetric operator is a densely defined linear operator with $\langle Ax,y\rangle=\langle x,Ay\rangle$ on its domain.
definition: A symmetric operator on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ is a linear [operator](c:operator) $A$ defined on a dense subspace $D(A)$ with $\langle Ax,y\rangle=\langle x,Ay\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(A)$. Equivalently, $A$ is a restriction of its [adjoint](c:adjoint-operator): $A\subseteq A^*$.
examples: The operator $-i\,d/dx$ on $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)\subset L^2(\mathbb R)$ is symmetric, because integration by parts has no boundary term.
Every Hermitian matrix is a symmetric operator on $\mathbb C^n$ with domain all of $\mathbb C^n$.

Non-example: $-i\,d/dx$ on $C^\infty[0,1]$ with no boundary condition is not symmetric, because $\langle Af,g\rangle-\langle f,Ag\rangle=-i\big(f(1)\overline{g(1)}-f(0)\overline{g(0)}\big)$ is not zero in general.

steps: Let $A$ be a [self-adjoint operator](c:self-adjoint-operator), so $A=A^*$ with the same domain.
Since $A^*y=Ay$ for $y\in D(A)$, we get $\langle Ax,y\rangle=\langle x,Ay\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(A)$.
So $A$ is symmetric; a symmetric operator only needs $D(A)\subseteq D(A^*)$ and may have a smaller domain than its adjoint.
links.why: Every self-adjoint operator is symmetric, and the gap between $D(A)$ and $D(A^*)$ is why self-adjoint extensions are a question.

reminder: $\mathrm{Tor}_n^R(M,N)$ is the $n$-th homology of a projective resolution of $M$ tensored with $N$.
definition: For a ring $R$ and $R$-[modules](c:module) $M$ and $N$, $\mathrm{Tor}_n^R(M,N)$ is the $n$-th homology of the [chain complex](c:chain-complex) $P_\bullet\otimes_RN$, where $P_\bullet\to M$ is a resolution of $M$ by [projective modules](c:projective-module). These groups are the left [derived functors](c:derived-functor-in-homological-algebra) of the [tensor product](c:tensor-product), and they do not depend on the choice of resolution.
examples: We have $\mathrm{Tor}_0^R(M,N)=M\otimes_RN$, and $\mathrm{Tor}_n^R(M,N)=0$ for $n>0$ when $M$ or $N$ is flat.
For the integers, $\mathrm{Tor}_1^{\mathbb Z}(\mathbb Z/n,\mathbb Z/m)\cong\mathbb Z/\gcd(n,m)$.

Non-example: The plain tensor product $-\otimes\mathbb Z/2$ is not Tor: it is not exact, since it sends the injection $\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb Z$ to the zero map, and $\mathrm{Tor}_1$ records this failure.

steps: Fix an $R$-module $N$ and take the right exact functor $F=-\otimes_RN$.
Choose a projective resolution $P_\bullet\to M$ and apply $F$ to $P_\bullet$.
The left [derived functor](c:derived-functor-in-homological-algebra) $L_nF(M)$ is the $n$-th homology of $F(P_\bullet)$, which is $\mathrm{Tor}_n^R(M,N)$.
links.why: General facts about derived functors, such as long exact sequences, give long exact sequences for Tor.

reminder: A [graph](c:graph) is triangle-free when no three of its [vertices](c:vertex) are all joined to each other.
definition: A [graph](c:graph) is triangle-free when it has no [clique](c:clique) of three [vertices](c:vertex), that is, no three vertices are joined to each other by all three possible edges.
examples: Every bipartite graph is triangle-free, for example the complete bipartite graph $K_{m,n}$.
The cycle $C_5$ and the Petersen graph are triangle-free, but they are not bipartite.
Non-example: The complete graph $K_4$ contains a triangle on any three of its vertices.

steps: Let $G$ be a [bipartite graph](c:bipartite-graph) with parts $U$ and $V$, so every edge joins $U$ to $V$.
Take any three vertices of $G$; two of them lie in the same part.
These two vertices are not adjacent, so the three vertices do not form a triangle.
links.why: Every bipartite graph is triangle-free, but the cycle $C_5$ shows that triangle-free is a weaker condition.

reminder: A trigonometric polynomial is a finite sum of constant multiples of $\cos kx$ and $\sin kx$ for whole numbers $k$.
definition: A trigonometric polynomial of degree at most $N$ is a function $T(x)=a_0+\sum_{k=1}^N(a_k\cos kx+b_k\sin kx)$ with constants $a_k$ and $b_k$. It is a finite partial sum of a [Fourier series](c:fourier-series), and so it is a $2\pi$-[periodic function](c:periodic-function) built from [trigonometric functions](c:trigonometric-function).
examples: The function $\cos^2x=\tfrac12+\tfrac12\cos2x$ is a trigonometric polynomial of degree $2$.
The Dirichlet kernel $D_N(x)=\sum_{k=-N}^Ne^{ikx}$ is a trigonometric polynomial of degree $N$.
Non-example: $\cos(x/2)$ is not a trigonometric polynomial, because its frequency $1/2$ is not a whole number and it has no period $2\pi$.

steps: Write $T(x)=\sum_{k=-N}^Nc_ke^{ikx}$ for a trigonometric polynomial $T$.
By orthogonality, the Fourier coefficient $\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}T(x)e^{-imx}\,dx$ equals $c_m$ for $|m|\le N$ and $0$ otherwise.
So the [Fourier series](c:fourier-series) of $T$ is $T$ itself, a series with only finitely many nonzero terms.
links.why: A trigonometric polynomial is a Fourier series that stops, so Fourier tools apply with no convergence questions.

reminder: A tube domain is a set of points in $\mathbb C^n$ whose imaginary parts lie in a fixed open set.
definition: A tube domain in the space $\mathbb C^n$ of $n$-tuples of [complex numbers](c:complex-number) is a set $T_B=\{x+iy:\ x\in\mathbb R^n,\ y\in B\}$, where the base $B\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is a [connected](c:connected-space) [open set](c:open-set). The real part $x$ of a point is free, and only the imaginary part $y$ must lie in $B$.
examples: The upper half-plane $\{x+iy:y>0\}$ is a tube domain in $\mathbb C$ with base $(0,\infty)$.
The future tube $\{x+iy\in\mathbb C^4:y\in V_+\}$ over the open forward light cone $V_+$ is a tube domain.
Non-example: The open unit disc in $\mathbb C$ is not a tube domain, because whether $x+iy$ lies in it depends on $x$ as well as on $y$.

reminder: A function is uniformly continuous when one $\delta$ works for each $\varepsilon$ at every point of the domain.
definition: A function $f:X\to Y$ between [metric spaces](c:metric-space) is uniformly continuous when for every $\varepsilon>0$ some $\delta>0$ gives $d(f(x),f(x'))<\varepsilon$ whenever $d(x,x')<\delta$, for all $x,x'\in X$. The number $\delta$ depends on $\varepsilon$ only and not on the point, which is the difference from a plain [continuous function](c:continuous-function).
examples: Every Lipschitz function is uniformly continuous, for example $\sin x$ on $\mathbb R$ with $\delta=\varepsilon$.
Every continuous function on a compact metric space is uniformly continuous, by the Heine-Cantor theorem.
Non-example: $f(x)=x^2$ on $\mathbb R$ is not uniformly continuous, because $f(n+1/n)-f(n)>2$ while the distance $1/n$ tends to $0$.

steps: Let $f$ be uniformly continuous, and fix a point $a$ and a number $\varepsilon>0$.
Take $\delta$ from uniform continuity; it works for all points, so it works at $a$.
Then $d(x,a)<\delta$ implies $d(f(x),f(a))<\varepsilon$, so $f$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) at $a$.
links.why: The extra condition is that $\delta$ depends on $\varepsilon$ alone, and this is what extension and compactness arguments use.

steps: Let $f$ be [Lipschitz continuous](c:lipschitz-continuous-function), so $d(f(x),f(x'))\le L\,d(x,x')$ with $L>0$.
Given $\varepsilon>0$, put $\delta=\varepsilon/L$.
If $d(x,x')<\delta$, then $d(f(x),f(x'))<L\delta=\varepsilon$ for all $x$ and $x'$.
links.why: Every Lipschitz function is uniformly continuous, but $\sqrt x$ on $[0,1]$ shows that the converse fails.

reminder: The Weyl group is the finite group generated by the reflections in the roots of a root system.
definition: The Weyl group of a [root system](c:is-root-system) $\Phi$ is the finite group generated by the [reflections](c:reflection-at-a-hyperplane) in the hyperplanes orthogonal to the roots. For a connected [compact Lie group](c:compact-lie-group) $G$ with [maximal torus](c:maximal-torus) $T$, it is the [quotient group](c:quotient-group) $N_G(T)/T$ of the normalizer of $T$ by $T$.
examples: For $\mathrm{SU}(n)$, whose root system has type $A_{n-1}$, the Weyl group is the symmetric group $S_n$, which permutes the diagonal entries of the maximal torus.
For $\mathrm{SO}(3)$, with root system $A_1$, the Weyl group is $\mathbb Z/2$, generated by one reflection.
Non-example: The cyclic group of order $3$ acting by rotations on the plane is not a Weyl group, because it contains no reflection.

steps: Choose simple roots $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r$ of the root system and let $s_i$ be the reflection in $\alpha_i$.
The $s_i$ generate $W$, and the relations $(s_is_j)^{m_{ij}}=1$ with $m_{ij}\in\{2,3,4,6\}$ define $W$.
A [Coxeter group](c:coxeter-group) allows any $m_{ij}$ in $\{2,3,\dots,\infty\}$, so $W$ is the finite crystallographic case.
links.why: Presentation and length facts about Coxeter groups, such as reduced words, carry over to Weyl groups.

steps: A [reflection group](c:reflection-group) is a group of linear maps of a Euclidean space generated by reflections.
The Weyl group is generated by the reflections $s_\alpha$ in the hyperplanes orthogonal to the roots $\alpha$.
The root system adds the crystallographic condition that $2(\alpha,\beta)/(\beta,\beta)$ is an integer for all roots $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
links.why: Facts about finite reflection groups, such as the chamber structure, apply to Weyl groups.

reminder: Points are affinely independent when none of them is an affine combination of the others.
definition: Points $v_0,\dots,v_k$ of a [vector space](c:vector-space) are affinely independent when the vectors $v_1-v_0,\dots,v_k-v_0$ are [linearly independent](c:linear-independence). Equivalently, $\sum\lambda_iv_i=0$ and $\sum\lambda_i=0$ force every $\lambda_i=0$.
examples: Any two distinct points, and any three points of a plane that are not on one line, are affinely independent.
The points $0,e_1,\dots,e_n$ of $\mathbb R^n$ are affinely independent; they are the vertices of a simplex.
Non-example: The points $(0,0)$, $(1,1)$ and $(2,2)$ are not affinely independent, because $(2,2)=2(1,1)-(0,0)$.

steps: Let $v_0,\dots,v_k$ be [linearly independent](c:linear-independence) vectors, and suppose $\sum\lambda_iv_i=0$ with $\sum\lambda_i=0$.
Linear independence forces every $\lambda_i=0$.
So the points are affinely independent, since affine independence asks the same only for coefficients with sum $0$.
links.why: Linearly independent vectors give affinely independent points, but the points $0$ and $e_1$ show that the converse fails.

reminder: An algebra over a [monad](c:monad) $T$ is an object $A$ with a map $TA\to A$ that respects the unit and the multiplication.
definition: An algebra over a [monad](c:monad) $(T,\mu,\eta)$ on a [category](c:category) $\mathcal C$ is an object $A$ with a structure map $a:TA\to A$ such that $a\circ\eta_A=\mathrm{id}_A$ and $a\circ Ta=a\circ\mu_A$. A morphism of algebras is a map $f:A\to B$ with $f\circ a=b\circ Tf$.
examples: For the list monad on Sets, an algebra is a monoid: the structure map $\mathrm{List}(A)\to A$ multiplies a list of elements.
For the power-set monad on Sets, an algebra is a complete join-semilattice, with the structure map taking the join of a subset.
For the monad $M\times-$ on Sets, with $M$ a monoid, an algebra is a set with a left action of $M$.
Non-example: The map $\mathrm{List}(\mathbb N)\to\mathbb N$ that sends a list to its length is not an algebra of the list monad, because it breaks the unit law: $a([5])=1\ne5$.

steps: Take an [algebra over a Lawvere theory](c:algebra-over-a-lawvere-theory) $\mathbb L$, with the forgetful functor from algebras to Sets.
This functor has a left adjoint, and the induced monad $T$ on Sets is finitary.
The algebras of $\mathbb L$ are exactly the algebras over $T$, so every Lawvere algebra is a monad algebra.
links.why: Monad algebras also cover infinitary structures, such as complete lattices, that no Lawvere theory describes.

steps: Forget the monad structure and keep only the underlying endofunctor $T$ of $\mathcal C$.
An [algebra for the endofunctor](c:algebra-for-an-endofunctor) $T$ is an object $A$ with a map $a:TA\to A$.
A monad algebra is such an algebra that also satisfies the unit law and the multiplication law.
links.why: Constructions for algebras of endofunctors apply, and the two laws are the extra condition.

reminder: An algebraic integer is a complex number that is a root of a monic polynomial with integer coefficients.
definition: A [complex number](c:complex-number) $\alpha$ is an algebraic integer when it is a [root](c:root-of-a-polynomial) of a [monic polynomial](c:monic-polynomial) with [integer](c:integer) coefficients. The algebraic integers of a number field form its ring of integers.
examples: The number $\sqrt2$ is an algebraic integer, because it is a root of $x^2-2$.
The golden ratio $(1+\sqrt5)/2$ is an algebraic integer, because it is a root of $x^2-x-1$.
Non-example: The number $1/2$ is not an algebraic integer, because a rational root of a monic integer polynomial must be an integer.

steps: Let $n$ be an [integer](c:integer).
Then $n$ is a root of the monic polynomial $x-n$, which has integer coefficients.
So every integer is an algebraic integer, and the rational algebraic integers are exactly the integers.
links.why: Algebraic integers carry the ideas of divisibility and primes from the integers to number fields.

reminder: An almost complex structure is a smooth choice of a linear map $J$ on each tangent space with $J^2=-\mathrm{id}$.
definition: An almost complex structure on a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ is a smooth field of linear maps $J:TM\to TM$ on the [tangent bundle](c:tangent-bundle) with $J^2=-\mathrm{id}$. It makes each tangent space a complex vector space, with $J$ acting as multiplication by $i$.
examples: Every complex manifold has one: $J$ acts as multiplication by $i$ on each tangent space.
On $\mathbb R^{2n}$ the map $J(x,y)=(-y,x)$ is an almost complex structure.
The sphere $S^6$ has an almost complex structure, built from the octonions.
Non-example: No odd-dimensional manifold has one, because $J^2=-\mathrm{id}$ would give $(\det J)^2=-1$ on an odd-dimensional tangent space.

steps: Let $M$ be a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) with holomorphic coordinates $z_j=x_j+iy_j$.
Define $J\partial_{x_j}=\partial_{y_j}$ and $J\partial_{y_j}=-\partial_{x_j}$ on each chart.
Then $J^2=-\mathrm{id}$, and $J$ does not depend on the chart, because the transition maps are holomorphic.
links.why: Every complex manifold carries an almost complex structure, but an almost complex structure comes from complex charts only when it is integrable.

reminder: The amalgamated product $A\ast_CB$ glues two groups along a common subgroup $C$, with no other relations.
definition: Let $A$ and $B$ be groups and let $\iota_A:C\to A$ and $\iota_B:C\to B$ be [group homomorphisms](c:group-homomorphism), usually injective. The amalgamated free product $A\ast_CB$ is the [quotient](c:quotient-group) of the [free product](c:free-product-of-groups) $A\ast B$ by the [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup) generated by all $\iota_A(c)\iota_B(c)^{-1}$.
examples: The group $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$ is the amalgamated product $\mathbb Z/4\ast_{\mathbb Z/2}\mathbb Z/6$.
For a space $X=U\cup V$ with $U$, $V$ and $U\cap V$ open and path connected, the fundamental group of $X$ is $\pi_1(U)\ast_{\pi_1(U\cap V)}\pi_1(V)$, by the Seifert-van Kampen theorem.
Non-example: With $C$ trivial, $A\ast_CB$ is the free product, not the direct product: in $\mathbb Z\ast\mathbb Z$ the two generators do not commute.

steps: Take $C$ to be the trivial group, with its unique homomorphisms into $A$ and $B$.
Then each element $\iota_A(c)\iota_B(c)^{-1}$ is the identity, so the normal subgroup it generates is trivial.
So $A\ast_1B$ equals the [free product](c:free-product-of-groups) $A\ast B$.
links.why: Free products are the case with no identification, and the general case glues along a shared subgroup.

reminder: An analytic continuation extends a holomorphic function to a larger connected open set, and the extension is unique.
definition: Let $f$ be a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) on a connected [open set](c:open-set) $U\subseteq\mathbb C$, and let $V\supseteq U$ be a larger connected open set. An analytic continuation of $f$ to $V$ is a holomorphic function $g$ on $V$ with $g=f$ on $U$, and it is unique when it exists.
examples: The series $\sum_{n\ge0}z^n$ on $|z|<1$ continues to $1/(1-z)$ on $\mathbb C\setminus\{1\}$.
The Gamma function, given by an integral for $\mathrm{Re}\,z>0$, continues to $\mathbb C$ minus the poles $0,-1,-2,\dots$.
Non-example: The series $\sum_{n\ge0}z^{2^n}$ has no analytic continuation to any larger open set, because every point of the unit circle is a singularity.

reminder: An associated prime of $N$ is a [prime ideal](c:prime-ideal) that is the radical of $(N:x)$ for some element $x$.
definition: Let $N$ be a [submodule](c:submodule) of a [module](c:module) $M$ over a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$, and write $(N:x)=\{r\in R:rx\in N\}$. A [prime ideal](c:prime-ideal) $I$ of $R$ is an associated prime of $N$ when $I$ is the [radical](c:radical) of $(N:x)$ for some $x\in M$. The textbook form asks for $I=(N:x)$ itself.
examples: For $R=M=\mathbb Z$ and $N=12\mathbb Z$, the ideals $(2)$ and $(3)$ are associated primes: $(N:6)=(2)$ and $(N:4)=(3)$.
For $R=M=k[x,y]$ and $N=(x^2,xy)$, the ideals $(x)$ and $(x,y)$ are associated primes: $(N:y)=(x)$ and $(N:x)=(x,y)$.
Non-example: For $R=M=\mathbb Z$ and $N=12\mathbb Z$, the prime $(5)$ is not associated, because $(N:x)$ is the ideal generated by $12/\gcd(12,x)$, and its radical is never $(5)$.

reminder: An associative algebra is a vector space with a bilinear and associative product.
definition: An associative algebra over a field $k$ is a [vector space](c:vector-space) $A$ with a [bilinear map](c:bilinear-map) $A\times A\to A$, written as a product, that is [associative](c:associative-operation): $(ab)c=a(bc)$. Usually one also asks for a unit $1$ with $1a=a=a1$.
examples: The matrix algebra $M_n(k)$ with matrix multiplication is an associative algebra of dimension $n^2$.
The polynomial ring $k[x]$, and the algebra $\mathrm{End}(V)$ of linear maps of a vector space $V$, are associative algebras.
Non-example: $\mathbb R^3$ with the cross product is bilinear but not associative, because $(e_1\times e_1)\times e_2=0$ and $e_1\times(e_1\times e_2)=-e_2$.

steps: A [nonassociative algebra](c:nonassociative-algebra) is a vector space $A$ with a bilinear product $A\times A\to A$.
Impose the extra condition $(ab)c=a(bc)$ for all $a$, $b$ and $c$.
The result is an associative algebra.
links.why: Associativity is the extra condition, and it makes powers, matrices and representations well behaved.

reminder: The Bernoulli numbers are the rational numbers $B_n$ with $t/(e^t-1)=\sum B_nt^n/n!$.
definition: The Bernoulli numbers $B_n$ are the [rational numbers](c:rational-number) for which $t/(e^t-1)$ is their exponential [generating function](c:generating-function): $\frac{t}{e^t-1}=\sum_{n\ge0}B_n\frac{t^n}{n!}$, where $e^t$ is the [exponential function](c:exponential-function). With this convention $B_1=-1/2$.
examples: The first values are $B_0=1$, $B_1=-\tfrac12$, $B_2=\tfrac16$ and $B_4=-\tfrac1{30}$, and $B_n=0$ for odd $n\ge3$.
Euler's formula $\zeta(2k)=(-1)^{k+1}\dfrac{B_{2k}(2\pi)^{2k}}{2\,(2k)!}$ gives the zeta values at even integers.
Non-example: The sequence $1,1,1,\dots$ is not the Bernoulli sequence, because its generating function $\sum t^n/n!=e^t$ differs from $t/(e^t-1)$.

reminder: SAT asks whether some assignment of truth values makes a given propositional formula true.
definition: The Boolean satisfiability problem asks, for a given formula of [propositional logic](c:propositional-logic), whether some assignment of truth values to its variables makes the formula true. It is a decision problem: for each input formula the answer is yes or no, and the formulas are built with the operations of a [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra).
examples: The formula $(p\vee q)\wedge\neg p$ is satisfiable: the assignment $p=\mathrm{false}$, $q=\mathrm{true}$ makes it true.
The formula $p\wedge\neg p$ is an input with the answer no, because no assignment makes it true.
Non-example: Counting the satisfying assignments is a different problem, called $\#\mathrm{SAT}$, because its answer is a number and not yes or no.

reminder: A bounded linear operator is a linear map $T$ with $\|Tx\|\le M\|x\|$ for one constant $M$.
definition: A bounded linear operator is a [linear map](c:linear-map) $T:X\to Y$ between [normed spaces](c:normed-space) for which some constant $M\ge0$ gives $\|Tx\|\le M\|x\|$ for all $x\in X$. The least such $M$ is the operator norm of $T$.
examples: Every linear map on a finite-dimensional normed space is bounded, for example every matrix acting on $\mathbb R^n$.
The right shift on $\ell^2$ is a bounded linear operator with $M=1$.
Non-example: Differentiation $d/dx$ from $C^1[0,1]$ to $C[0,1]$ with the sup norm is linear but not bounded, because $x^n$ has norm $1$ and its derivative has norm $n$.

steps: Start with a [linear map](c:linear-map) $T:X\to Y$ between normed spaces.
Add the condition that $\|Tx\|\le M\|x\|$ for some constant $M$ and all $x$.
If $X$ has finite dimension this condition always holds, so the two notions agree there.
links.why: Boundedness is the extra condition that makes a linear map continuous and gives it an operator norm.

reminder: The Cameron-Martin space of a Gaussian measure is the set of shifts that keep the measure absolutely continuous.
definition: Let $\gamma$ be a centered [Gaussian measure](c:gaussian-measure) on a [separable Banach space](c:separable-banach-space) $E$. Its Cameron-Martin space is the set of $h\in E$ for which the shifted measure $\gamma(\cdot-h)$ is [absolutely continuous](c:absolutely-continuous-measure) with respect to $\gamma$. This set is a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) with its own norm, and it sits inside $E$.
examples: For Wiener measure on $C_0[0,1]$, the Cameron-Martin space is the set of absolutely continuous $h$ with $h(0)=0$ and $h'\in L^2$, with norm $\|h'\|_{L^2}$.
For the standard Gaussian measure on $\mathbb R^n$, the Cameron-Martin space is all of $\mathbb R^n$.
Non-example: A typical Brownian path is not in the Cameron-Martin space, because with probability one it is nowhere differentiable, so $h'\notin L^2$.

reminder: The canonical bundle of an $n$-dimensional [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) is the [line bundle](c:line-bundle) of holomorphic $n$-forms.
definition: For a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) $X$ of dimension $n$, the canonical bundle $K_X$ is the [line bundle](c:line-bundle) of holomorphic $n$-forms, the top exterior power $\Lambda^nT^*X$ of the [cotangent bundle](c:cotangent-bundle). A local section is $f\,dz_1\wedge\dots\wedge dz_n$, a holomorphic [differential form](c:differential-form) of top degree.
examples: On the projective line $\mathbb P^1$ the canonical bundle is $\mathcal O(-2)$, and on $\mathbb P^n$ it is $\mathcal O(-n-1)$.
On a complex torus $\mathbb C^n/\Lambda$ the canonical bundle is trivial, since $dz_1\wedge\dots\wedge dz_n$ is a nowhere zero section.
Non-example: The cotangent bundle $T^*X$ of an $n$-dimensional complex manifold with $n\ge2$ is not the canonical bundle, because it has rank $n$ and not rank $1$.

reminder: The [commutator](c:commutator) of the position operator $q$ and the momentum operator $p$ equals $i\hbar$ times the identity.
definition: The canonical commutation relations are the identities $[q_j,p_k]=i\hbar\,\delta_{jk}$ and $[q_j,q_k]=0=[p_j,p_k]$ for position [operators](c:operator) $q_j$ and momentum operators $p_k$, where $[A,B]=AB-BA$ is the [commutator](c:commutator). For creation and annihilation operators they read $[a_j,a_k^*]=\delta_{jk}$ and $[a_j,a_k]=0$.
examples: On $L^2(\mathbb R)$ the operators $q=x$ and $p=-i\hbar\,d/dx$ satisfy $[q,p]f=i\hbar f$ for smooth rapidly decaying $f$.
The ladder operators $a$ and $a^*$ of the harmonic oscillator satisfy $[a,a^*]=1$.
Non-example: Finite matrices cannot satisfy $[A,B]=I$, because taking traces gives $0=\mathrm{tr}[A,B]=\mathrm{tr}\,I=n\ne0$.

reminder: In the canonical ensemble a state with energy $E$ has probability proportional to $e^{-E/(k_BT)}$.
definition: The canonical ensemble is the [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) on the states of a system in thermal equilibrium with a heat bath at fixed temperature $T$: a state $s$ with energy $E(s)$, the value of the [Hamiltonian](c:hamiltonian), has probability $e^{-\beta E(s)}/Z$ with $\beta=1/(k_BT)$. The normalizing constant $Z$ is the [partition function](c:partition-function).
examples: A two-level system with energies $0$ and $\epsilon$ has $P(\epsilon)=e^{-\beta\epsilon}/(1+e^{-\beta\epsilon})$.
The Ising model at inverse temperature $\beta$ gives each spin configuration $\sigma$ the weight $e^{-\beta H(\sigma)}/Z$.
Non-example: The microcanonical ensemble fixes the energy exactly and gives all states of that energy equal probability, so it is not canonical.

reminder: Čech cohomology computes cohomology of a space from cochains on open covers and takes a limit over finer covers.
definition: For a [sheaf](c:sheaf) $\mathcal F$ of abelian groups on a space $X$ and an [open cover](c:open-cover) $\mathcal U=(U_i)$, the Čech complex has $p$-cochains that give a section of $\mathcal F$ on each $(p+1)$-fold intersection $U_{i_0}\cap\dots\cap U_{i_p}$. The Čech [cohomology](c:cohomology) $\check H^p(X,\mathcal F)$ is the [colimit](c:colimit) over refinements of the cover of the cohomology of these complexes.
examples: For a good open cover of a manifold, Čech cohomology with constant coefficients equals singular cohomology.
The group $\check H^1(X,\mathcal O^*)$ classifies the line bundles on $X$.
Non-example: The trivial cover $\{X\}$ alone gives $\check H^p=0$ for $p>0$, which misses $\check H^1(S^1,\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$, so the limit over finer covers is needed.

reminder: The center of a group or ring is the set of elements that commute with every element.
definition: The center of an algebraic object $A$ such as a [group](c:group), a [monoid](c:monoid) or a [ring](c:ring) is the set $Z(A)=\{z\in A:za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\}$ of elements that commute with every element of $A$. The center is always commutative.
examples: The center of $\mathrm{GL}_n(k)$ is the group of nonzero scalar matrices $\lambda I$.
A group $G$ equals its center exactly when $G$ is abelian.
The center of the quaternion group $Q_8$ is $\{1,-1\}$.
Non-example: In $S_3$ the transposition $(1\,2)$ is not central, because $(1\,2)(1\,3)\ne(1\,3)(1\,2)$.

reminder: A configuration of a [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) records its current control state, its [tape](c:tape) contents and its head position.
definition: A configuration of a [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) is a snapshot of a computation: the current control state together with the [tape](c:tape), that is, its cell contents and the head position. A step of the machine maps one configuration to the next, and a run is a sequence of configurations.
examples: The initial configuration on input $w$ has the start state and a tape holding $w$ with the head on its first symbol.
A halting configuration is one for which the machine has no next step.
Non-example: The transition table of the machine is not a configuration, because it stays the same at every step while a configuration changes.

reminder: The characteristic polynomial of a square matrix $A$ is $\det(tI-A)$, and its roots are the eigenvalues of $A$.
definition: The characteristic polynomial of a square [matrix](c:matrix) $A$ is the [polynomial](c:polynomial) $p_A(t)=\det(tI-A)$, where $\det$ is the [determinant](c:determinant). It is monic of degree $n$ for an $n\times n$ matrix, and its roots are the [eigenvalues](c:eigenvalue) of $A$.
examples: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ the characteristic polynomial is $(t-2)(t-3)$.
For $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ it is $t^2-(a+d)t+(ad-bc)$, and for a rotation by $\theta$ it is $t^2-2\cos\theta\,t+1$.
Non-example: The minimal polynomial is not the characteristic polynomial: for $A=I_2$ the minimal polynomial is $t-1$, but the characteristic polynomial is $(t-1)^2$.

reminder: A chi-squared variable with $k$ degrees of freedom is a sum of $k$ squared independent standard normal variables.
definition: The chi-squared distribution with $k$ degrees of freedom is the distribution of $Z_1^2+\dots+Z_k^2$, where $Z_1,\dots,Z_k$ are [independent random variables](c:independent-random-variables) with the standard [normal distribution](c:normal-distribution). It equals the [gamma distribution](c:gamma-distribution) with shape $k/2$ and scale $2$.
examples: For $k=1$ it is the distribution of $Z^2$ for one standard normal $Z$; in general the mean is $k$ and the variance is $2k$.
For a normal sample of size $n$ with variance $\sigma^2$, the quantity $(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2$ has the chi-squared distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom.
Non-example: If $Z_2=Z_1$, then $Z_1^2+Z_2^2=2Z_1^2$ is not chi-squared with $2$ degrees of freedom, because the summands must be independent.

steps: The [gamma distribution](c:gamma-distribution) with shape $a$ and scale $\theta$ has a density proportional to $x^{a-1}e^{-x/\theta}$ on $x>0$.
Choose $a=k/2$ and $\theta=2$.
The density becomes proportional to $x^{k/2-1}e^{-x/2}$, the chi-squared density with $k$ degrees of freedom.
links.why: Facts about gamma distributions, such as sums of independent variables, give facts about chi-squared variables.

reminder: The circulation of a vector field around a closed curve is the line integral of the field along the curve.
definition: The circulation of a [vector field](c:vector-field) $\mathbf v$ around an oriented [closed curve](c:closed-curve) $C$ is the [line integral](c:line-integral) $\Gamma=\oint_C\mathbf v\cdot d\mathbf r$ of the component of $\mathbf v$ along $C$.
examples: For the rotation field $\mathbf v=(-y,x)$ and the unit circle taken counterclockwise, the circulation is $2\pi$.
A gradient field $\nabla\phi$ has circulation $0$ around every closed curve.
Non-example: The line integral of $\mathbf v$ along an open arc is not a circulation, because a circulation needs a closed curve.

steps: Take a vector field $\mathbf v$ and the [line integral](c:line-integral) $\int_C\mathbf v\cdot d\mathbf r$ along a curve $C$.
Require that $C$ is closed, so that it ends at the point where it starts.
The line integral of $\mathbf v$ over this closed curve is the circulation $\Gamma$.
links.why: Circulation is the closed-curve case, which is where Stokes-type theorems and conservative fields apply.

reminder: A closed geodesic is a geodesic that returns to its starting point with its starting velocity.
definition: A closed geodesic on a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) $M$ is a [geodesic](c:geodesic) $\gamma:\mathbb R\to M$ that is periodic, so $\gamma(t+T)=\gamma(t)$ for some $T>0$. It traces a smooth [closed curve](c:closed-curve), because the velocity returns to its starting value too.
examples: The great circles of the unit sphere $S^2$ are closed geodesics of length $2\pi$.
On the flat torus $\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$, the straight lines of rational slope are closed geodesics.
Non-example: On the flat torus, a line of irrational slope is a geodesic that never closes up, so it is not a closed geodesic.

steps: Take a [geodesic](c:geodesic) $\gamma$ on the Riemannian manifold $M$.
Add the condition $\gamma(t+T)=\gamma(t)$ for some period $T>0$.
Then $\gamma$ traces a closed curve, and it is a closed geodesic.
links.why: Closed geodesics are the periodic geodesics, which trace formulas and the prime geodesic theorem count.

reminder: A closed subspace is a subset whose complement is open, taken with the subspace topology.
definition: A closed subspace of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is a [subset](c:subset) $C\subseteq X$ whose [complement](c:complement) is an [open set](c:open-set) of $X$, taken with the [subspace topology](c:subspace-topology). Equivalently, $C$ contains all its limit points.
examples: The interval $[0,1]$ is a closed subspace of $\mathbb R$, and the $x$-axis is a closed subspace of $\mathbb R^2$.
Every finite-dimensional linear subspace of a normed space is a closed subspace.
Non-example: The interval $(0,1]$ is not closed in $\mathbb R$, because $0$ is a limit point that lies outside it.

reminder: A coalgebra is a vector space with a coassociative comultiplication and a counit, the dual notion to an algebra.
definition: A coalgebra over a field $k$ is a [vector space](c:vector-space) $C$ with linear maps $\Delta:C\to C\otimes C$ into the [tensor product](c:tensor-product) and $\varepsilon:C\to k$, such that $\Delta$ is [coassociative](c:co-associativity) and $\varepsilon$ is a [counit](c:co-unitality) for $\Delta$. It is the notion obtained from an [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) by reversing the arrows of the product and the unit.
examples: For a set $X$, the vector space $kX$ with basis $X$ is a coalgebra with $\Delta(x)=x\otimes x$ and $\varepsilon(x)=1$.
The dual $A^*$ of a finite-dimensional algebra $A$ is a coalgebra.

Non-example: On $k^2$ the map with $\Delta(e_1)=\Delta(e_2)=e_1\otimes e_2$ is not coassociative, since $(\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta(e_1)=e_1\otimes e_2\otimes e_2$ but $(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta)\Delta(e_1)=e_1\otimes e_1\otimes e_2$.

steps: A [comonoid](c:comonoid) in a monoidal category has a comultiplication $\Delta:C\to C\otimes C$ and a counit $\varepsilon:C\to I$.
Take the monoidal category of vector spaces over $k$, with the tensor product and the unit object $k$.
Coassociativity and the counit laws then become exactly the conditions on a coalgebra over $k$.
links.why: Statements about comonoids in any monoidal category apply to coalgebras, and other categories give other kinds of coalgebra.

reminder: A coherent sheaf is a sheaf of modules that is locally finitely generated and has locally finitely generated relations.
definition: A coherent sheaf on a ringed space $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ is a [sheaf of modules](c:module-sheaf) $\mathcal F$ that is locally generated by finitely many sections and whose local relations are again locally finitely generated. Over an affine open piece it comes from a [coherent module](c:coherent-module), which on a Noetherian [scheme](c:scheme) is just a finitely generated module.
examples: The structure sheaf $\mathcal O_X$ of a Noetherian scheme is coherent.
Vector bundles, that is, locally free sheaves of finite rank, are coherent sheaves.
Non-example: The infinite direct sum $\mathcal O_X^{\oplus\mathbb N}$ on a nonempty scheme is quasi-coherent but not coherent, because no finite set of local sections generates it.

steps: Start with a [sheaf of modules](c:module-sheaf) $\mathcal F$ over the structure sheaf $\mathcal O_X$.
Require that every point has a neighborhood where finitely many sections generate $\mathcal F$.
Require also that the kernel of every map $\mathcal O_U^n\to\mathcal F|_U$ is again locally finitely generated.
links.why: Coherence adds the finiteness that makes cohomology finite and rank and degree defined.

reminder: A combinatorial line in $A^n$ is the set of words made from one template by putting the same letter into all its wildcards.
definition: Let $A$ be a [finite set](c:finite-set), the alphabet, and let $n\ge1$. A combinatorial line in $A^n$ is a set $\{w(a):a\in A\}$ of [words](c:word) of length $n$, where $w$ is a word over $A\cup\{*\}$ with at least one wildcard $*$, and $w(a)$ replaces every $*$ by the letter $a$.
examples: For $A=\{0,1,2\}$ and $n=3$, the template $1{*}2$ gives the line $\{102,112,122\}$.
For the same $A$ and $n$, the template $*0*$ gives the line $\{000,101,202\}$, in which both wildcards take the same letter.
